recipes.name: CLIP cannot do NEGATION in a positive prompt
recipes.claim: CLIP cannot do NEGATION in a positive prompt — 'no hat', 'without a scar' often ADD the thing you wanted gone.
recipes.summary: CLIP processes the semantic content of tokens, not their logical relationship to 'no'/'not'/'without'. The word 'hat' activates the hat concept regardless of a nearby 'no'. Diffusion's separate negative-prompt channel exists precisely because the positive encoder has no negation operator — the negative prompt steers CFG AWAY from those concepts, which is a different mechanism than understanding 'not'.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: NEVER write exclusions in the positive prompt. Put the bare concept to avoid in the NEGATIVE prompt field ('hat', 'scar', 'jewelry') — not 'no hat', not 'without scar'. State only what you WANT positively. For 'an empty room' prefer affirmative phrasing of the desired state over 'a room with no people'.

recipes.name: Non-depictable / narrative tokens DILUTE the embedding
recipes.claim: Non-depictable / narrative tokens DILUTE the embedding — abstractions like 'worn by grief', 'guarded and steady', backstory consume token budget and weaken the visual ones.
recipes.summary: CLIP (and the studio's failure case) only have embeddings for concepts it saw paired with IMAGES. 'Grief', 'guarded', 'why the patch is faded' have no stable visual grounding, so they don't add a coherent direction — but they DO occupy positions in the 77-token budget and dilute the averaged/bagged concept set, pulling the result toward the generic mean. This is the same mechanism that mushed the T5 prose prompt, and it's WORSE in CLIP given the ~20-token effective window.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Translate every emotional/narrative beat into a VISIBLE cue before it enters a CLIP prompt. 'Worn by grief' -> 'dark under-eye circles, hollow cheeks, downturned mouth'. 'Guarded and steady' -> 'arms crossed, level gaze, squared stance'. 'Faded patch' -> 'frayed cloth patch, bleached fabric'. Cut pure backstory entirely from the image prompt — keep it in the character bible, not the encoder input. Every token must name something a camera could capture.

recipes.name: Token ORDER and front-loading materially change the image
recipes.claim: Token ORDER and front-loading materially change the image — earlier tokens dominate.
recipes.summary: Two compounding causes: (1) only the first ~20 positional embeddings are well-trained (effective-length finding), and (2) practitioners consistently observe earlier tokens exert more influence on the result. A defining attribute placed at the end of a long prompt can have near-zero effect. NOTE: the claim 'earlier = strictly more weight by positional encoding math' is partly FOLKLORE — the dominance is real and reproducible, but it's driven by training-data position bias + effective-length decay, not a clean monotonic weighting law. Treat 'front-load' as a strong heuristic, not a precise dial.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Order tokens by importance, most-important first: subject -> key attributes -> medium/style -> secondary details -> background. To strengthen a concept, MOVE it earlier before reaching for (token:1.3) weighting. Build a fixed studio template slot order so every character prompt front-loads identity consistently.

recipes.name: Cross-attention has a FIXED budget
recipes.claim: Cross-attention has a FIXED budget: every added token competes for the same attention mass, so non-visual words measurably starve the visual ones (attention dilution is real, not folklore).
recipes.summary: Zhang et al. (Attention Regulation) show cross-attention layers 'disproportionately focus on certain tokens', and that correct generations have attention EVENLY distributed across the relevant tokens while failures show a few tokens dominating and others 'neglected'. Because softmax attention sums to 1 across all prompt tokens, adding a backstory clause does not add a new channel — it redistributes a fixed pie. The narrative tokens, having no visual referent, still consume attention mass and pull it away from 'olive jacket' and 'red scar'. This is the literal mechanism of the studio's T5 failure: the grief-prose didn't just fail to help, it actively diluted the depictable tokens.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Treat the prompt as a zero-sum attention budget. Spend every token on a visible attribute. Cut filler ('a person who is', 'we can see that', 'the kind of'), connective backstory, and mood-prose — each one steals attention from a feature you actually want rendered. Shorter, denser, all-visual prompts render more faithfully than long narrative ones.

recipes.name: LLM-based encoders (Qwen2.5-VL for Qwen-Image, Qwen3-4B for…
recipes.claim: LLM-based encoders (Qwen2.5-VL for Qwen-Image, Qwen3-4B for Z-Image) parse structure, negation and relations FAR better than CLIP — but they reward a different prompt SHAPE (detailed structured description, often via a system-prompt rewrite).
recipes.summary: Qwen-Image (Qwen2.5-VL) and Z-Image (Qwen3-4B) feed an actual LLM's hidden states as conditioning. Because Qwen2.5-VL is vision-language ALIGNED and Qwen3 is a strong instruction LM, these encoders retain syntax, count, spatial relations, and negation that CLIP destroys. Qwen-Image is explicitly trained/used with a system prompt that REWRITES the user prompt into a dense, detailed, structured description (the recommended 'magic prompt' path produces short-summary + medium-detail + object tags + long fine-grained caption). So the failure mode flips: terse tag-soup underperforms; rich, well-organized depictable description wins — and it tolerates structure CLIP can't. Still text/LLM, still no benefit from un-depictable intent: backstory remains inert.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: For Qwen-Image / Z-Image, write a structured, paragraph-style visual description (subject → appearance → clothing/material → pose → lighting → framing), and lean on the model's prompt-rewrite/system-prompt path rather than fighting it with SDXL-style comma tags. You may use clear spatial/relational/negation phrasing here ('standing to the left of the crate, no helmet') — these encoders handle it. Keep it all visible: structure is rewarded, mood-prose still is not.

recipes.name: Token limits are HARD and truncation is SILENT
recipes.claim: Token limits are HARD and truncation is SILENT — work past them and the tail of your prompt (often the most specific details, placed last) is simply discarded.
recipes.summary: CLIP-L and OpenCLIP-bigG: 77 tokens including BOS/EOS (≈75 usable), ≈300-375 chars at ~4-5 chars/token; diffusers truncates and warns, but in many UIs the warning is unseen. ComfyUI/A1111 don't truncate — they CHUNK into 75-token blocks, encode each separately, and concatenate, so cross-block attribute binding is lost (a detail in chunk 2 cannot bind to a subject in chunk 1); 'BREAK' forces a chunk boundary. T5-XXL: 512 tokens on FLUX.1-dev/Chroma, but only 256 on FLUX.1-schnell, and you must pass max_sequence_length=512 or it silently caps lower. Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image): effectively no practical prompt cap (32k context, YaRN-extendable). Qwen3-4B (Z-Image): large LLM context, no 77-style cap. The danger: writers front-load mood-prose and the truncator eats the depictable specifics at the end.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Budget consciously per target. SDXL: keep the whole prompt under ~75 tokens (~300 chars) and put load-bearing visible attributes FIRST so nothing critical is in the truncated tail; avoid relying on BREAK-split details binding across chunks. FLUX-dev/Chroma: stay under 512 tokens and explicitly set max_sequence_length=512; on schnell assume a 256-token wall. Qwen/Z-Image: length is not the constraint — depictability and structure are.

recipes.name: piling on quality tokens ('masterpiece, ultra-detailed…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE, DEBUNKED: piling on quality tokens ('masterpiece, ultra-detailed face, 8k, sharp facial features, perfect face, highly detailed') does NOT add face pixels — and on CLIP it can crowd the face descriptor past the ~20-token effective window.
recipes.summary: 'Detailed face' / 'portrait' style tokens are real and mildly helpful — community testing shows 'detailed face' nudges rendering quality — but they operate on the diffusion prior's notion of 'a nice face,' not on the latent resolution allocated to the face region. They cannot recover detail the VAE discarded (Finding 1), cannot supply a specific identity (Finding 2), and on SDXL each extra quality token pushes real descriptors toward the dead zone past token ~20 (Finding 3). The folklore is treating these as a substitute for framing/upscaling; they are a garnish, not the meal.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]
recipes.design_implication: Allow ONE face-quality token max ('detailed face' or 'sharp facial features') and put it early; do not stack a quality-token wall. The actual levers for a hero face, in priority order: (1) framing so the head gets >=512px, (2) a face-detailer/upscale pass on the crop, (3) IP-Adapter/InstantID for identity, (4) then — last and least — a single face-quality token. If you're adding the 4th token to fix a problem, you skipped levers 1-3.

recipes.name: Reference-conditioning (IP-Adapter/FaceID/InstantID) runs…
recipes.claim: Reference-conditioning (IP-Adapter/FaceID/InstantID) runs on a SEPARATE cross-attention path from text and can be weighted independently — face strength is a knob, not a word.
recipes.summary: IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention adds dedicated image-feature attention layers parallel to the text layers; InstantID adds IdentityNet (face embedding as 'strong semantic' + 5 facial landmarks as 'weak spatial' control). Both expose an adapter/conditioning scale. This means likeness fidelity is controlled by the adapter weight and the landmark map, fully decoupled from prompt wording — you can crank face fidelity without touching the text, and over-cranking InstantID landmarks over-constrains pose (loss of editability), which is why it uses only 5 keypoints.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Tune the hero's likeness with the ADAPTER scale (IP-Adapter weight / InstantID IdentityNet strength), not by adding more face adjectives to the prompt. If the face is right but the pose is locked/stiff, lower the InstantID landmark/spatial weight rather than rewording. Keep text doing pose+scene+wardrobe; keep the adapter doing identity; tune them on independent dials.

recipes.name: T5's full 512-token budget is OPT-IN
recipes.claim: T5's full 512-token budget is OPT-IN: many runners leave max_sequence_length at 256, silently truncating the back half of a long character prompt.
recipes.summary: FLUX.1-dev/SD3 T5 supports 512 tokens but FLUX.1-schnell caps at 256, and several diffusers code paths default to 256 even on dev. Truncation past max_sequence_length is silent — no error. So a carefully ordered prompt where the face/wardrobe detail sits in the second half can have that half vanish entirely if the runner didn't set 512. Unlike CLIP, there's no effective-length collapse, so the fix is purely 'use the budget you paid for.'  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Explicitly set max_sequence_length=512 in the T5/FLUX/Chroma pipeline, and STILL order the prompt face-first as insurance: subject + face + identity descriptors before scene/lore. On Schnell (256 cap), be ruthless — there is no room for prose at all; depictables only.

recipes.name: The official 'positive magic' quality tail is a real,…
recipes.claim: The official 'positive magic' quality tail is a real, specific string — not arbitrary booru spam.
recipes.summary: Qwen-Image's own examples append, in English: ', Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition.' and in Chinese: ', 超清，4K，电影级构图.'. Because the LLM reads these as trailing descriptive clauses (not isolated tags), a short, grammatical quality tail integrates cleanly; a long pile of disconnected quality tags ('masterpiece, best quality, intricate, hyperdetailed, 8k, award winning...') is the CLIP-era habit that does NOT match how this causal encoder reads.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Append the short official magic tail (', Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition.') and STOP. Do not stack 10+ quality tags — on an LLM encoder they dilute, they don't stack. For CJK prompts use the Chinese magic string, not the English one.

recipes.name: Qwen-Image's encoder is Qwen2.5-VL
recipes.claim: Qwen-Image's encoder is Qwen2.5-VL — a full VLM — deliberately chosen OVER T5 and over the plain Qwen3 LLM.
recipes.summary: The technical report gives three reasons: (1) Qwen2.5-VL's language and visual spaces are already aligned, making it better suited to T2I than language-only encoders like Qwen3; (2) it retains strong language-modeling ability without degradation; (3) its multimodal input unlocks editing. Conditioning is the last-layer hidden state (encoder_hidden_states.hidden_states[-1]) of the LLM backbone — NOT a pooled CLIP embedding and NOT T5's bidirectional encoder output. This is a causal, autoregressive read of your prompt, so word ORDER and grammatical structure carry real weight, unlike a CLIP bag-of-concepts.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Write Qwen-Image prompts as well-formed, ordered natural-language sentences, not comma-salad tags. Put the most important subject/composition facts FIRST — the causal LLM reads left-to-right and early tokens anchor the scene. Do not port an SDXL Danbooru tag string verbatim.

recipes.name: Z-Image's encoder is Qwen3-4B
recipes.claim: Z-Image's encoder is Qwen3-4B — a pure LLM (no vision) — chosen for bilingual instruction-alignment and efficiency, with conditioning from the SECOND-to-last hidden layer (dim 2560).
recipes.summary: The Z-Image paper: 'we employ the lightweight Qwen3-4B as the text encoder, leveraging its bilingual proficiency to align complex instructions with visual content.' Reference code takes hidden_states[-2] (2560-dim) as conditioning — NOT the last layer (unlike Qwen-Image's hidden_states[-1]). Text and image tokens are concatenated into one S3-DiT stream but separated by 3D RoPE axes (text increments on the temporal axis, image on spatial), so text and image don't compete for positions.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Treat Z-Image like a small, literal instruction-follower: clear, declarative, bilingual-friendly natural language. It is a 4B LLM, not a frontier model — keep instructions concrete and unambiguous; don't rely on subtle world-knowledge or implication the way you might with a large chat model.

recipes.name: CFG scale ranges are model-family-specific and NOT…
recipes.claim: CFG scale ranges are model-family-specific and NOT interchangeable — a value that's correct on SDXL fries FLUX and is meaningless on a turbo model.
recipes.summary: Practical ranges, grounded in vendor/community guidance: SDXL-CLIP true CFG ~4-7 (start 5-6; 9+ over-sharpens/saturates — Rescale-CFG ~0.7 if you must go high). Chroma (de-distilled FLUX, T5) runs TRUE CFG and honors negatives, typically ~4-6. Qwen-Image base ~3-5 true CFG. FLUX-dev: real cfg_scale=1, with a SEPARATE distilled 'guidance' embedding ~3.5 (<=3.5 photoreal, 3.5-6 illustration) — this guidance knob is NOT CFG and does not enable negatives. FLUX-schnell / SDXL-Turbo / SDXL-Lightning / LCM / Z-Image-Turbo: cfg_scale=1 fixed, no negatives — use NAG/PAG for control. The common mistake is carrying an SD1.5 CFG~7-9 habit forward, which over-guides SDXL and 'causes chaos in Flux.'  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Set CFG per family in the studio presets, never globally: SDXL 5-6 (cap 7, add RescaleCFG 0.7 above that); Chroma 4-6 with real negatives; Qwen-Image base 3-5; FLUX-dev real-CFG 1 + distilled-guidance 3.5; all turbo/schnell/LCM/Z-Image-Turbo CFG 1 + NAG/PAG for any negative-style control. Don't reuse one number across the rig — wrong CFG is the most common cause of both fried and washed-out JRPG art.

recipes.name: copy-pasted 50-80 word negative blocklists ('worst quality,…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE: copy-pasted 50-80 word negative blocklists ('worst quality, low quality, jpeg artifacts, ugly, bad hands...') are mostly cargo cult — token competition dilutes each term and several terms are inert.
recipes.summary: Mechanically, the negative prompt is a single embedding; cramming dozens of concepts in spreads the limited 'avoidance' across all of them, so each term gets a weak directional contribution (and on CLIP models, past 77 tokens the tail is truncated entirely). Terms like 'worst quality/low quality' only do anything if the base/finetune was captioned with those literal phrases (true for many SD1.5/anime models, largely NOT for SDXL base, FLUX, Qwen, Z-Image) — otherwise they are near-random directions. Community testing repeatedly shows SDXL/SD3.5 often improve with SHORTER negatives, and removing irrelevant terms lets the model focus avoidance energy on the ones that matter. The mathematically reliable lever is weighting/embeddings, not word count.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Delete the inherited mega-negative. Use 3-8 targeted terms max, each one a concept actually present-and-unwanted in YOUR positive's direction (for 2.5D cel art: 'photorealistic, 3d render, photograph, blurry'). Drop 'worst quality/low quality' on SDXL/FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image unless you verified that finetune was trained on those tags. If a term needs to bite harder, weight it ((term:1.3)) rather than adding ten cousins of it. Audit the studio's preset negatives — most are probably dead weight.

recipes.name: PAG (Perturbed-Attention Guidance) is the other…
recipes.claim: PAG (Perturbed-Attention Guidance) is the other distilled-model workaround, but it is a STRUCTURE/quality booster, not a true negative — it needs no negative prompt at all and works even at CFG=1.
recipes.summary: PAG (Ahn et al. 2024, arXiv:2403.17377) creates a deliberately structurally-degraded version of the prediction by replacing selected self-attention maps in the U-Net with an identity matrix, then guides AWAY from that degraded sample. Because the 'thing to avoid' is generated internally (not from a text negative), PAG works in unconditional generation and at guidance_scale=0/1 — exactly the regime where CFG/negatives are dead. diffusers' default pag_scale=3.0 'works well in most cases'; too-high pag_scale itself causes smoother textures and slight saturation (same failure family as CFG). Crucially PAG cannot suppress a SPECIFIC concept (it has no semantic target) — it only repairs anatomy/composition coherence. So for distilled models: use PAG to fix wonky hands/structure, use NAG to suppress a named attribute.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: On turbo/distilled JRPG renders with anatomy or composition glitches but no specific thing to ban, enable PAG (pag_scale ~3.0) rather than stacking 'bad anatomy, extra fingers' into a dead negative field. Use PAG for 'make it cleaner/coherent'; reach for NAG only when you must ban a NAMED concept. Don't crank pag_scale past ~4-5 or you reintroduce the saturated look.

recipes.name: MINIMAL DEFENSIBLE DEFAULTS per family
recipes.claim: MINIMAL DEFENSIBLE DEFAULTS per family: short depictable lists only where true CFG exists; empty everywhere distillation killed it. High-CFG SDXL also needs CFG-rescale, not more negatives, to fix burn.
recipes.summary: Synthesizing the above into shippable defaults for a 2.5D JRPG character pipeline. SDXL (CLIP, true CFG): default negative = 'lowres, blurry, watermark, text, signature, extra fingers, jpeg artifacts' -- 5-8 depictable defects, comma tags; if pushing CFG high for adherence, add CFG-rescale (Lin et al 2023, arXiv:2305.08891) ~0.7 to kill oversaturation rather than fighting burn with negatives. Chroma / FLUX-base (T5, true CFG): short prose negative 'blurry, low-detail, watermark or text overlay, deformed hands' -- one clause, not a tag dump. FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning: EMPTY negative, steer positively. Qwen-Image: empty-string ' ' negative, rely on positive + positive_magic. Always start nearer empty and add per-defect.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Ship these defaults: SDXL -> 'lowres, blurry, watermark, text, extra fingers, jpeg artifacts' (+ CFG-rescale 0.7 if CFG>7); Chroma/FLUX-base -> short clause 'blurry low-detail image, watermark or text, deformed hands'; FLUX-dev/schnell + Z-Image-Turbo + SDXL-Turbo -> empty; Qwen-Image -> empty string. Then trim/extend per observed defect.

recipes.name: The negative token must itself be DEPICTABLE (the…
recipes.claim: The negative token must itself be DEPICTABLE (the depictability law applies symmetrically). Abstract negatives like 'low quality', 'bad', 'amateur' do almost nothing.
recipes.summary: Negation works by mutual cancellation in latent space (arXiv:2406.02965): the negative prompt only deletes a concept if that concept has a strong, localizable visual representation whose noise can cancel the positive noise. 'blurry', 'lowres', 'jpeg artifacts', 'watermark', 'extra fingers' are depictable defects -- they map to coherent image features and cancel well. 'low quality'/'bad anatomy'/'masterpiece'(negated) are abstract aesthetic abstractions with no single visual locus, so they smear weak, diffuse pressure and mostly just reduce variety. arXiv:2601.08070 quantifies this: violation probability is predicted by the concept's baseline depictability/probability (P0), violation = sigma(-2.40 + 2.27*P0), 78% of variance -- low-pressure (rare/abstract) concepts the model wasn't going to draw anyway are 'suppressed' trivially (9% violation) while strongly-depicted concepts resist (46%).  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Only put depictable nouns/defects in negatives ('blur', 'watermark', 'text', 'six fingers'). Delete abstract aesthetic words ('low quality', 'bad', 'ugly', 'masterpiece') -- they waste tokens and flatten variety.

recipes.name: Qwen-Image is the trap
recipes.claim: Qwen-Image is the trap: it exposes a true_cfg_scale and REQUIRES a negative_prompt argument, yet the Qwen2.5-VL encoder was not trained for negative conditioning, so the negative is weak-to-inert even at true_cfg_scale > 1.
recipes.summary: Qwen-Image's pipeline takes true_cfg_scale (default ~4.0) which does run a real two-pass CFG, and the negative_prompt parameter is mandatory for the pipeline to execute. But because the text encoder is a generative VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) rather than a contrastive CLIP, the model lacks the trained push-away behavior; practitioner testing across CFG 1.0-7.0 found essentially zero exclusion effect. The negative_prompt exists as a pipeline placeholder, not a working lever. Qwen ships positive_magic suffixes (', Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition.') and recommends specifying intent positively. So: structurally it has CFG, behaviorally it ignores negatives like a distilled model.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: On Qwen-Image, set negative_prompt to an empty string (' ') -- do not invest effort in it. Steer entirely via a detailed positive prompt plus the official positive_magic suffix. Treat its negatives as cosmetic, not functional.

recipes.name: LICENSE / commercial-safety of these embeddings is UNVERIFIED
recipes.claim: LICENSE / commercial-safety of these embeddings is UNVERIFIED — most carry 'license: other' or vague Civitai custom terms with no explicit commercial grant. This is a real liability for a commercial studio.
recipes.summary: The gsdf/EasyNegative dataset card states 'license: other' with NO explicit commercial-use grant; the HF mirror is sometimes tagged CDLA-Permissive-2.0, but the two disagree, so provenance is ambiguous. Civitai model pages use a patchwork of CreativeML OpenRAIL-M, custom restrictive flags, and unspecified terms; there is no reliable license filter, and a TI embedding's training-data provenance is opaque. For a commercial product, shipping art steered by an asset whose license is 'other/unverified' and whose training set is unknown is an avoidable legal exposure.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: For commercial JRPG art, do NOT ship outputs that depend on third-party negative embeddings unless you have a written, explicit commercial grant AND known training-data provenance. EasyNegative et al. fail both (license: 'other', no commercial grant, opaque data). Default to plain-text negatives, which carry zero licensing surface, on your CFG-honoring base models.

recipes.name: Negatives share the SAME 77-token CLIP budget as the positive
recipes.claim: Negatives share the SAME 77-token CLIP budget as the positive — a bloated negative truncates silently and high CFG turns leftover negatives into burn.
recipes.summary: Each CLIP encoder caps at 77 tokens (75 usable + BOS/EOS); the negative prompt gets its OWN 77-token window but diffusers/most UIs TRUNCATE silently past it — so a 50-term megablock that overflows means later terms (often the 'important' ones a user appended) are dropped without warning. Separately, piling on negatives invites cranking CFG to 'make them bite,' but high CFG on SDXL/SD-lineage causes oversaturation/burnout — the exact failure Lin et al. 2023 (rescale-CFG, arXiv:2305.08891) document and fix. So 'long negative + high CFG' is a double cargo-cult: truncation loses terms AND the high CFG degrades the image. (T5 in Chroma/FLUX allows far longer context, so the 77-token truncation specifically is a CLIP-encoder problem.)  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Keep the negative well under 75 tokens on any CLIP model (SDXL) — assume silent truncation past it, so a 50-word block may be dropping your real terms. Don't raise CFG to compensate for a weak negative; if SDXL output looks oversaturated/burnt, apply CFG-rescale (Lin et al. 2023) rather than fighting it with more negatives.

recipes.name: To A/B a prompt change cleanly, LOCK the seed and change…
recipes.claim: To A/B a prompt change cleanly, LOCK the seed and change exactly ONE token. With z_T held fixed, every pixel difference is attributable to that one edit.
recipes.summary: Because the pipeline is deterministic given (seed, prompt, sampler, steps, CFG, resolution, model), fixing the seed and changing a single token isolates the causal effect of that token: composition stays roughly anchored by the shared z_T, so the delta you see is the edit's contribution, not noise. The official HuggingFace Diffusers guide builds its prompt-engineering workflow on exactly this — generate a batch, pick one, then 'keep the first seed so that the images are similar to the first image' while improving the prompt. This is how you learn what a token actually does in YOUR model before committing it to a production prompt. It also exposes silently-ignored tokens: if a one-token change under a locked seed produces zero visible difference, that token is being dropped by the encoder (a prompt-fixable signal, not a seed one).  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: When testing a prompt edit, freeze the seed (and sampler/steps/CFG/resolution/model) and change ONE token or phrase per generation — never the seed and the prompt together. Read the delta against the locked baseline. If the locked-seed edit moves the image -> the token is active, keep iterating on this seed. If it moves nothing -> the encoder is ignoring it; reword, reorder, or reweight rather than re-rolling.

recipes.name: magic seeds' that fix a bad prompt do not exist. 'Golden'…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE ZONE: 'magic seeds' that fix a bad prompt do not exist. 'Golden' seeds raise AVERAGE aesthetic quality a little — they cannot add a missing element a prompt never requested.
recipes.summary: The research that sounds like it supports magic seeds actually bounds them. 'Good Seed Makes a Good Crop' (arXiv 2405.14828) finds ~65-67 'golden' seeds whose aggregate FID is better (best 21.60 vs worst 31.97) and whose ranking partially generalizes across prompts — but that is a small statistical bump in overall image quality (sharpness, fewer artifacts), NOT a fix for content. No seed makes the model render an object you didn't ask for, bind an attribute the encoder dropped, or make a generic character magnetic. Seeds are also NOT portable across models or even across model versions/schedulers — the same number indexes a different noise field per RNG/model, so a seed someone shares as 'amazing' carries no guarantee in your stack. Treat any claim of a seed that 'fixes prompts' or 'works everywhere' as folklore.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]
recipes.design_implication: Never hunt for a magic seed to fix a content miss — it is a category error and wastes render time (this is exactly the 'generic nobody' trap). Do not trust shared/borrowed 'great seeds' across models, versions, or schedulers; re-derive your own. The only legitimate seed search is batching for the best COMPOSITION under an already-correct prompt — and even then the quality gain is marginal vs fixing the prompt.

recipes.name: The seed is the initial noise latent (z_T)
recipes.claim: The seed is the initial noise latent (z_T); the prompt is the cross-attention conditioning. They control different things — the seed seeds the COMPOSITION, the prompt steers the CONTENT.
recipes.summary: In latent diffusion (Rombach 2022), generation starts from a random Gaussian latent z_T selected by the seed, and a U-Net iteratively denoises it toward z_0; the text prompt enters only as a conditioning signal through cross-attention layers at each denoising step (Ho 2020 DDPM is the underlying reverse process). The denoising trajectory is therefore a function of BOTH inputs: the same seed + same prompt is fully deterministic (identical pixels), so any change in output is attributable to exactly one of the two knobs. This is the mechanical basis for the whole re-roll-vs-rewrite decision: re-rolling swaps z_T (a new structural starting point, same semantic instruction); rewriting changes the instruction (same or new starting point). Confusing the two is the root error behind the 'generic slouching nobody' incident — re-rendering and tweaking tonemaps changes neither z_T's semantics nor the conditioning in a way that fixes a content miss.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Before touching anything on a bad result, name the defect as either COMPOSITION (a property of this z_T: pose, framing, object placement, hand layout, this particular face) or CONTENT (a property of the instruction: a missing element, wrong style, ignored attribute, generic-when-asked-specific). Composition defect -> re-roll the seed. Content defect -> rewrite the prompt. Never tweak render/tonemap/lighting to fix either — those touch neither z_T nor the conditioning.

recipes.name: CFG scale — not the seed — is the dial for 'follow the…
recipes.claim: CFG scale — not the seed — is the dial for 'follow the prompt harder'. When a character is generic/off-identity, raising CFG (within a sane band) increases prompt adherence; re-rolling the seed cannot.
recipes.summary: Classifier-free guidance combines the conditional and unconditional model predictions with a guidance weight: higher CFG pushes the output toward the prompt, lower CFG makes it more diverse/random. The seed is orthogonal to this — it picks the noise, CFG picks how hard the noise is bent toward the prompt. A guidance range around 4-10 (defaults ~7-8 for many SDXL-era models) balances adherence vs diversity; FLUX/distilled and Qwen/Z-Image families use their own much lower 'distilled guidance' scales, so the band is model-specific.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: When the SUBJECT is under-rendered or generic, before re-rolling: (1) strengthen the identity tokens in the prompt, then (2) nudge CFG up toward the upper end of the model's band (SDXL ~7-9). If raising CFG makes it fried/over-saturated instead of more on-prompt, the prompt itself lacks the identity content — fix the prompt. Use the model-appropriate CFG band (do not apply SDXL's CFG 7 to FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image distilled-guidance, which want much lower values). The seed is the LAST lever, only after subject and CFG are right.

recipes.name: there is no UNIVERSAL magic/lucky seed. 'Golden' seeds…
recipes.claim: FOLKLORE ZONE: there is no UNIVERSAL magic/lucky seed. 'Golden' seeds measurably exist but the quality gap is modest and the ranking is model-specific — seed quality is conditional, not magic.
recipes.summary: The one empirical study on this (Xu et al., 'Good Seed Makes a Good Crop', arXiv:2405.14828) found the best 'golden' seed scored FID 21.60 vs the worst 'inferior' seed 31.97 on SD 2.0 — a real but bounded ~48% gap, and the seed rankings were derived PER MODEL (separate golden seeds for SD 2.0 vs SDXL Turbo). The paper itself admits the mechanism is opaque ('it is unclear what makes seeds easily discernible'). So a seed can bias toward better average composition/quality for a given model+prompt-set, but no seed is a portable cheat code that makes any prompt good. The community 'this seed always gives great faces' claim is folklore: it survives only within one fixed model+prompt+resolution+sampler configuration.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Do NOT maintain a personal 'lucky seed' list and expect it to improve unrelated prompts. Treat seeds as interchangeable lottery tickets within a config. If you want a quality edge, do a quick seed-sweep (e.g. 8-16 seeds) for a SPECIFIC frozen prompt+model and pick the winner FOR THAT shot only — never carry it forward as a universal asset. Quality lives in the prompt, model, and CFG, not in a blessed integer.

recipes.name: The seed only sets the START of the denoising trajectory…
recipes.claim: The seed only sets the START of the denoising trajectory (the initial noise latent); the PROMPT + CFG decide WHAT subject/identity/composition the trajectory converges toward. A generic-nobody character is a prompt miss, not a seed miss.
recipes.summary: In latent diffusion (Rombach 2022) the seed seeds the RNG that fills the initial Gaussian noise tensor — it picks one starting point in latent space. The reverse/denoising process (DDPM, Ho 2020) is then STEERED at every step by text conditioning injected through cross-attention, amplified by classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans 2022): the final score = unconditional + CFG*(conditional - unconditional). So the seed answers 'which of many valid images for THIS prompt', while the prompt+CFG answer 'what is in the image at all'. If the subject is wrong/generic/slouching, re-rolling the seed just samples a different generic-nobody from the same wrong prompt distribution. The operator's wasted re-render + tonemap tweaks were treating a conditioning failure as a sampling failure.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: DECISION RULE on a bad result: if the image is COMPETENT but you wanted a different pose/crop/variation of the SAME correct subject -> re-roll the seed. If the SUBJECT, identity, body language, or composition is wrong (generic nobody, wrong silhouette, missing the character's defining traits) -> STOP re-rolling, rewrite the prompt and/or raise CFG. Seed re-rolls cannot fix a conditioning miss. Add the character's load-bearing identity tokens (silhouette, posture, signature features) and confirm CFG is in the 4-8 adherence band before touching the seed.

recipes.name: Same seed + edited prompt = global structure preserved with…
recipes.claim: Same seed + edited prompt = global structure preserved with changed content, which is the controlled way to A/B test a prompt edit.
recipes.summary: Holding the seed fixed and changing only the prompt keeps the broad layout/pose/color basin roughly stable while swapping the semantic content (e.g., change one emotion word -> expression changes, hair/clothes/background largely persist). This is because the trajectory starts from the same z_T and only the conditioning vector differs, so early structure is shared before the prompt pulls content apart. This isolates the variable: you SEE what your word change actually did.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: When tuning prompt wording, FREEZE the seed (and use a deterministic sampler) and change one phrase at a time -- this turns 'did my edit help?' from guesswork into a clean before/after. Once the wording is right, THEN unfreeze the seed and batch-roll to pick the best instance. Freeze-seed for prompt science; roll-seed for instance selection.

recipes.name: The seed primarily fixes COMPOSITION, POSE, FRAMING, and…
recipes.claim: The seed primarily fixes COMPOSITION, POSE, FRAMING, and the specific face/identity instance; the prompt fixes WHAT content, attributes, and style are allowed.
recipes.summary: Because the initial noise determines where the model finds 'hooks' to grow structure, the seed strongly correlates with object arrangement, camera angle, body pose, and which specific face/instance is sampled. The prompt is the semantic constraint set: it says 'armored knight, scar, determined expression' but does not by itself pick which of infinitely many valid knights you get. Empirically, low-level traits (color palette, object pose, layout) persist across prompts when the noise is held fixed, while the prompt governs identity of content and style.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Diagnose by category. POSE / FRAMING / LAYOUT / which-face-you-got = SEED territory (re-roll). WHAT the character IS (clothing, age, expression descriptors, art style, mood) = PROMPT territory (rewrite). A 'generic slouching nobody' is two things: 'slouching' is partly seed (pose), but 'nobody / generic' is a PROMPT miss -- you never told it who this person is.

recipes.name: BREAK and 75-token chunking are CLIP-ONLY plumbing
recipes.claim: BREAK and 75-token chunking are CLIP-ONLY plumbing — concatenated chunks don't cross-attend, so split by semantic group, not mid-phrase.
recipes.summary: A1111/ComfyUI handle >75-token CLIP prompts by cutting into 75-token chunks, padding each with BOS/EOS, encoding independently, and concatenating along the sequence axis. Tokens in different chunks never attend to each other and weights don't cross the boundary. BREAK forces the cut where you want it (pads the current chunk, starts fresh). FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image have NO chunking — BREAK is meaningless text to them.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: On SDXL only: if you must exceed 75 tokens, insert BREAK at semantic seams (e.g. after the full character block, before the environment block) so related attributes stay in one chunk and don't get severed mid-phrase. Do not rely on chunk 2+ for critical attributes — cross-chunk binding is weak. On FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image: never type BREAK; just write a tight prompt under the cap.

recipes.name: Hard token limits differ wildly per encoder and ALL…
recipes.claim: Hard token limits differ wildly per encoder and ALL truncate the tail SILENTLY — schnell at 256 is the trap.
recipes.summary: Caps: CLIP 77 (75 usable), FLUX-dev T5 512, FLUX-schnell T5 256, Chroma T5 ~512, Qwen-Image 1024 default, Z-Image 512 (1024 local). None raise an error — the tail past the cap is dropped silently. FLUX-schnell's 256-token cap is half of dev's and bites mid-prompt on character sheets; a long description can lose its back half before encoding.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Pin a per-encoder character budget and order prompts so the most important content is always before the cap: CLIP first ~75 chars critical / ~300 hard; schnell ~1000 chars; dev/Chroma/Z-Image ~2000 chars; Qwen-Image ~3000+ chars. Put a token counter in the pipeline; never assume a prompt 'fit.' Verify Qwen-Image runs at max_sequence_length=1024 (diffusers bug #12075 caused RoPE artifacts from wrong padding).

recipes.name: Prompt weighting (word:1.3) is a CLIP/embedding-scaling trick
recipes.claim: Prompt weighting (word:1.3) is a CLIP/embedding-scaling trick — it does NOT transfer to T5 or LLM encoders.
recipes.summary: Weighting in A1111/ComfyUI/compel works by scaling the CLIP token embedding vectors before they reach the U-Net (compel interpolates toward/away from the empty-prompt embedding; ComfyUI applies a literal multiplier on the embedding). There is no equivalent learned hook in T5 or in LLM encoders (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3) — typing '(word:1.3)' into a FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image prompt just inserts literal parenthesis-and-number TOKENS that the encoder reads as text, usually degrading the result. Also note A1111 normalizes weights while ComfyUI uses a raw multiplier, so the same syntax differs across UIs.  [grounding: strong-community]
recipes.design_implication: Use (term:1.1-1.3) weighting ONLY on SDXL/CLIP. On T5 (FLUX/Chroma) and LLM encoders (Qwen-Image, Z-Image), emphasize via NATURAL LANGUAGE instead: repeat or foreground the concept, use stronger adjectives, or restructure the sentence ('the central focus is X'). Strip all weighting parentheses out of FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image prompts. Keep SDXL weights gentle (<=1.3); high weights fry the embedding.

recipes.name: FLUX splits labor
recipes.claim: FLUX splits labor: T5 supplies per-token fine-grained semantics fed into the transformer's joint attention; CLIP-L supplies only ONE pooled global vector folded into modulation/timestep — so CLIP carries the gist, T5 carries the detail.
recipes.summary: In FLUX/MMDiT, the T5 token sequence is concatenated with the noised image latents and participates in joint attention (the encoder that actually 'draws' the described content). CLIP-L contributes a single pooled embedding concatenated with the timestep embedding via the modulation pathway — a coarse global style/vibe signal, not per-word grounding. This is why CLIP's 77-token limit barely matters in FLUX: only the gist survives anyway.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: Put your full descriptive scene in the T5 prompt (it's what gets drawn). If your tool exposes a separate CLIP/clip_l field (CLIPTextEncodeFlux), put only a short global gist there (subject + overall style) — do not duplicate the whole paragraph; CLIP only keeps a pooled summary.

recipes.name: T5 is a full encoder-decoder language model with a…
recipes.claim: T5 is a full encoder-decoder language model with a BIDIRECTIONAL encoder trained on natural-language denoising — it genuinely parses grammar, clauses, and relations; CLIP does not.
recipes.summary: T5 (Raffel et al. 2020) uses a BERT-style fully-visible (bidirectional) encoder pre-trained with span-corruption on the C4 corpus, optimized for sentence-level semantics and contextual dependencies. Diffusion uses only the T5 ENCODER stack to produce per-token contextual embeddings. CLIP's text encoder, by contrast, is a causal contrastive model that empirically behaves like a bag-of-words and fails on attribute binding, relations, counting, and negation.  [grounding: empirical-paper]
recipes.design_implication: For T5 (FLUX/Chroma) write real sentences with grammar: 'a knight holding a cracked shield in her LEFT hand, looking over her shoulder.' T5 honors syntax — word order, prepositions, and clauses encode spatial/relational meaning. Save comma-separated keyword salad for the SDXL/CLIP lane.

recipes.name: T5-XXL in FLUX-dev/Chroma reads 512 tokens
recipes.claim: T5-XXL in FLUX-dev/Chroma reads 512 tokens; FLUX-schnell is hard-capped at 256; Chroma's INPAINT path silently defaults to 256, not 512.
recipes.summary: diffusers FluxPipeline defaults max_sequence_length=512 for dev (no hard cap) and forbids >256 for schnell. ChromaPipeline + ChromaImg2ImgPipeline default to 512, but ChromaInpaintPipeline's signature defaults to max_sequence_length=256. All paths use T5TokenizerFast on google/t5-v1_1-xxl. The token budget is roughly 1.3-1.5 tokens/English-word and ~3.5-4 chars/token, so 512 tokens ≈ 340-390 words ≈ 1,800 chars; 256 ≈ ~180 words.  [grounding: official-docs]
recipes.design_implication: Write the character/sprite prompt to fit ~350 words (1,800 chars) for FLUX-dev and Chroma txt2img; cut to ~180 words for FLUX-schnell. If you reuse a Chroma prompt for inpainting, PASS max_sequence_length=512 explicitly or it gets silently halved to 256.
